scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

Regular observance can cultivate habits of being forgiving and understanding, extending beyond the Lenten period into everyday life. 4. **Intentionality and Engagement**: The impact of these traditions depends on the level of engagement. Intentional reflection and growth during these periods can lead to genuine changes in attitude and behavior, whereas mere routine may not yield significant effects. 5. **Psychological Reinforcement**: Repetition can reinforce behaviors and attitudes. Consistent engagement in acts of reflection, forgiveness, and community can integrate into one's regular mindset, influencing their responsibilities towards others throughout the year. **Conclusion**: Annual religious observances can change one's perspective on their responsibilities towards others, especially when approached with depth and intentionality. These traditions provide consistent opportunities for reflection, growth, and community, potentially leading to more compassionate and responsible attitudes. The extent of their impact varies based on individual engagement and intentionality.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I should keep the $1100 I won at the family gathering or if I should give it back because it wasn't fair. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, the family gatherings are a big deal for us. We have a lot of cousins, and we all live close, so getting together is something we do often. My grandparents have this ranch where we usually meet, and it's become the go-to place for these gatherings. My uncles and older cousins are into sports, grilling, and gambling, so that's what we usually do when we get together. Gambling isn't really my thing, but I participate to be social. I usually lose money because I'm not as good at card games or knowing sports teams as everyone else. It's become a running joke among family members that I'm not great at gambling. This time, we had an especially large gathering. My aunt came up with a new idea for betting: a jar filled with beans. She said it was $20 a guess, and whoever guessed closest to the number of beans would take home all the money. Almost everyone participated, and some even made multiple guesses to increase their chances. Now, here's where I come in. I'm not usually good at gambling, but this time I was in my element. I figured out the jar was a typical 64 oz Mason jar, which I found out has a volume of 116 cubic inches. I also found out that a bean is about 0.15 cubic inches. Dividing the jar's volume by the bean's volume gave me about 773 beans. I assumed 20% of that was air, leaving me with around 619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and another for 630. When I was making my bets, people were teasing me, saying things like, "It'd be easier if you just gave it directly to me," but I just smiled and didn't say anything. Some people could tell something was up and kept giving me grief throughout the night. After about 40 minutes of counting, my aunt told everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anyone else's. At first, everyone was happy for me, laughing about how lucky I was. One of the suspicious cousins asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately, I could see people's faces start to sour. One of my uncles said, "That's bullshit," and left the room. In the end, I won nearly $1100. My parents told me I should offer to return it because I didn't earn it fairly. I argued that I had all the same information as everyone else. Now, I'm wondering if I'm being unfair by keeping the money. So, is it right or wrong for me to keep the money? Let's break this down. First, I used my knowledge of math and volume to estimate the number of beans in the jar. I made two guesses to increase my chances. I didn't cheat; I just used a different approach than everyone else. I had the same information as everyone else because the jar was visible, and the rules were clear. However, when I explained my strategy, people got upset. They felt that my method wasn't fair because it wasn't based on luck but on calculation. My uncle even left the room, which shows how upset he was. On one hand, I followed the rules, and my method was legitimate. I didn't cheat or manipulate the game in any way. On the other hand, the way I approached the game was different from everyone else's, and it made people uncomfortable because it wasn't based on chance but on skill. I also need to consider the impact on our family relationships. If I keep the money, it might cause hard feelings and tension at future gatherings. If I give it back, it might show that I value our family relationships more than the money, but it could also be seen as admitting that I did something wrong. Another thing to think about is the intention behind the game. My aunt created the game to make things simpler and more fun. By using a mathematical approach, I changed the nature of the game, making it less about chance and more about skill. This might have been against the spirit of the game, even if I didn't break any rules. I also need to consider the expectations of the other participants. Most people were participating based on luck and social interaction, not on mathematical calculations. By using a different approach, I altered the game's dynamics, which could be seen as unfair. In conclusion, while I technically followed the rules and didn't cheat, my approach changed the nature of the game and caused discomfort among family members. Keeping the money might be seen as taking advantage of the situation, even if unintentionally. Returning the money could help maintain harmony within the family and show that I value our relationships over the money.
